title: Convex sets
objectives: Prove a set is convex, including the set of long-only weights.

screens.title: Two discs
screens.prose: The shaded shape is two unit discs, centred at $(-1.5, 0)$ and $(1.5, 0)$. Drag A and B anywhere in it. Slide $\theta$ to move Q along the segment from B to A.

derive.caption: Q = $\theta$A + (1 − $\theta$)B is {{fixed(min(hypot(theta*A.x+(1-theta)*B.x+1.5, theta*A.y+(1-theta)*B.y), hypot(theta*A.x+(1-theta)*B.x-1.5, theta*A.y+(1-theta)*B.y)), 2)}} from the nearer centre: {{min(hypot(theta*A.x+(1-theta)*B.x+1.5, theta*A.y+(1-theta)*B.y), hypot(theta*A.x+(1-theta)*B.x-1.5, theta*A.y+(1-theta)*B.y)) <= 1.0001 ? 'inside' : 'outside'}} the shape.

screens.question: Put A and B on the two centres and set $\theta = 0.5$. How far is Q from each centre?

widget.accept: 1.5: the midpoint $(0, 0)$ is outside both discs.
widget.label: Distance from Q to a centre

hints.text: With $\theta = 0.5$, Q is the midpoint of A and B.
The midpoint of $(-1.5, 0)$ and $(1.5, 0)$ is the origin.
The origin is 1.5 from each centre, and each radius is 1.

feedback.correct: Q is 1.5 from each centre, more than the radius of 1. The segment leaves the shape.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put A at $(-1.5, 0)$, B at $(1.5, 0)$ and read Q at $\theta = 0.5$.

byKey.radius: 1 is the radius. Q at the origin is 1.5 from each centre.
byKey.gap: 3 is the distance between the centres. Q sits halfway, 1.5 from each.
byKey.zero: Q is not at a centre. With $\theta = 0.5$ it is the midpoint, the origin.

explain.text: With A and B on the centres, Q at $\theta = 0.5$ is the origin. It is 1.5 from each centre, so it lies in neither disc. Two points of the shape have a segment that leaves it.

screens.title: One ellipse
screens.prose: Now the shape is the ellipse $\tfrac{x^2}{4} + y^2 \le 1$. Try every pair of points you like, and every $\theta$ from 0 to 1.

derive.caption: Q is {{pow(theta*A.x+(1-theta)*B.x, 2)/4 + pow(theta*A.y+(1-theta)*B.y, 2) <= 1.0001 ? 'inside' : 'outside'}} the ellipse: $x^2/4 + y^2$ = {{fixed(pow(theta*A.x+(1-theta)*B.x, 2)/4 + pow(theta*A.y+(1-theta)*B.y, 2), 2)}}.

screens.question: Can Q leave the ellipse while A and B stay inside?

options.text: No. For any A and B inside and any $\theta$, Q stays inside.
Yes, when A and B sit at the two ends of the long axis.
options.why: You pictured $(\pm 2, 0)$, but the segment between them is the axis itself, which lies inside.

options.text: Yes, when $\theta$ is close to 0 or 1.
options.why: At $\theta = 0$ or 1, Q is B or A, and those you chose inside.

hints.text: Try the pair that broke the discs: two points far apart.
The ellipse has no dent between two points.
No segment between two points of the ellipse ever leaves it.

feedback.correct: Every segment stays in. A set with that property is called **convex**; the two discs are not convex.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Try A and B far apart and slide $\theta$ all the way.

byKey.ends: Put A at $(-2, 0)$ and B at $(2, 0)$. Q runs along the axis and never leaves.
byKey.theta: At the ends of the slider Q is A or B itself, so it is inside.

explain.text: A set is **convex** when the segment between any two of its points stays in it. The ellipse passes; the two discs fail at their centres.

screens.title: Long-only weights
screens.prose: Long-only, fully invested weights on three assets satisfy $w_i \ge 0$ and $w_1 + w_2 + w_3 = 1$. In 3D that set is a triangle; flat, we draw $(w_1, w_2)$ and read $w_3 = 1 - w_1 - w_2$. Take A $= (0.6, 0.3, 0.1)$ and B $= (0.1, 0.2, 0.7)$.
screens.question: At $\theta = 0.4$, Q $= \theta$A + $(1 - \theta)$B. What is its third weight $w_3$?

hints.text: Mix the third weights: $0.4 \times 0.1 + 0.6 \times 0.7$.
$\theta = 0.4$ goes on A and $1 - \theta = 0.6$ on B.

feedback.correct: $w_3 = 0.04 + 0.42 = 0.46$. Q $= (0.30, 0.24, 0.46)$ is still long-only and still sums to 1.

byKey.swap: You put $\theta$ on B: $0.4 \times 0.7 + 0.6 \times 0.1 = 0.34$. The weight $\theta$ goes on A.
byKey.added: You added the two third weights. A mix weights them by $\theta$ and $1 - \theta$.

explain.text: Q $= 0.4(0.6, 0.3, 0.1) + 0.6(0.1, 0.2, 0.7) = (0.30, 0.24, 0.46)$. Every entry is nonnegative and they sum to 1, so Q is on the triangle.

screens.title: Why the triangle passes
screens.prose: We now prove it for every pair and every $\theta$, not just one. Let $\Delta = \{\mathbf{w} : w_i \ge 0, \ \mathbf{1}^T\mathbf{w} = 1\}$.
screens.question: Put the proof that $\Delta$ is convex in order. Leave out the lines that do not belong.

lines.text: Each $w_i = \theta a_i + (1 - \theta)b_i$ is a sum of products of nonnegative numbers, so $w_i \ge 0$.
The entries sum to $\theta \cdot 1 + (1 - \theta) \cdot 1 = 1$, because each of $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ sums to 1.
So $\mathbf{w} \in \Delta$ for every pair and every $\theta$: $\Delta$ is convex.
The midpoint $\tfrac12\mathbf{a} + \tfrac12\mathbf{b}$ lies in $\Delta$, so $\Delta$ is convex.
lines.why: One value of $\theta$ is not every value. The definition asks for all $\theta$ in $[0, 1]$.
That is false: $w_i$ lies between $a_i$ and $b_i$, so it can exceed $a_i$.

hints.text: Start from two arbitrary points and an arbitrary $\theta$.
Two things to check: the signs and the sum.
Signs: nonnegative times nonnegative. Sum: $\theta + (1 - \theta) = 1$.

feedback.correct: Take two points, check the signs, check the sum, conclude. The signs and the sum can come in either order.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Begin with arbitrary $\mathbf{a}$, $\mathbf{b}$ and $\theta$, then check both conditions.

byKey.d1: Checking the midpoint tests $\theta = \tfrac12$ only. The proof must hold for every $\theta$.
byKey.d2: That step is false and not needed. $w_i$ is between $a_i$ and $b_i$.
byKey.left-out: You left out a step the proof needs: the start, the signs, the sum or the conclusion.

explain.text: Arbitrary points and an arbitrary $\theta$ make the proof cover every case. Nonnegative mixes of nonnegative numbers stay nonnegative. The budget survives because $\theta$ and $1 - \theta$ sum to 1.

screens.title: Caps cut the triangle
screens.prose:
A set $\{\mathbf{x} : \mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{x} \le b\}$ is a **half-space**; it is convex. A 50% cap $w_i \le 0.5$ is one. If $C_1$ and $C_2$ are convex, a segment between points of both stays in each:
$$\theta\mathbf{a} + (1 - \theta)\mathbf{b} \in C_1 \cap C_2.$$

state.caption: The inner triangle keeps every weight at most 50%. Its third edge is $w_3 = 0.5$.

screens.question: Why is the capped set (the inner triangle) convex?

options.text: It is the triangle cut by three half-spaces, and an intersection of convex sets is convex.
It is smaller than the triangle, and a part of a convex set is convex.
options.why: You assumed any part stays convex. Cut two far discs out of a big disc and the part is not.

options.text: Its three corners are long-only portfolios.
options.why: You checked three points. Convexity is about every segment, not the corners.

feedback.correct: Each cap is a half-space and the triangle is convex, so their intersection is convex. Its corners are $(\tfrac12, \tfrac12, 0)$, $(\tfrac12, 0, \tfrac12)$ and $(0, \tfrac12, \tfrac12)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Name the kind of set each cap is, and what happens when convex sets overlap.

byKey.smaller: A part of a convex set need not be convex. This part is an intersection, which is.
byKey.corners: Corners do not prove it. The intersection rule does.

explain.text: The caps $w_1 \le 0.5$, $w_2 \le 0.5$ and $w_3 \le 0.5$ are three half-spaces. Intersected with the triangle they leave the inner triangle with corners $(\tfrac12, \tfrac12, 0)$, $(\tfrac12, 0, \tfrac12)$ and $(0, \tfrac12, \tfrac12)$.

screens.title: A risk budget
screens.prose: Our three assets are uncorrelated with volatilities 20%, 30% and 40%, so $\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \operatorname{diag}(0.04, 0.09, 0.16)$. A risk budget $\mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{w} \le 0.04$ caps volatility at 20%. With $w_3 = 1 - w_1 - w_2$ it is the inside of an ellipse.

derive.caption: Volatility: A {{fixed(100*sqrt(0.04*A.x*A.x + 0.09*A.y*A.y + 0.16*(1-A.x-A.y)*(1-A.x-A.y)), 2)}}%, B {{fixed(100*sqrt(0.04*B.x*B.x + 0.09*B.y*B.y + 0.16*(1-B.x-B.y)*(1-B.x-B.y)), 2)}}%, Q {{fixed(100*sqrt(0.04*(theta*A.x+(1-theta)*B.x)*(theta*A.x+(1-theta)*B.x) + 0.09*(theta*A.y+(1-theta)*B.y)*(theta*A.y+(1-theta)*B.y) + 0.16*(1-(theta*A.x+(1-theta)*B.x)-(theta*A.y+(1-theta)*B.y))*(1-(theta*A.x+(1-theta)*B.x)-(theta*A.y+(1-theta)*B.y))), 2)}}%. The curve is 20%.

screens.question: What is the volatility of A $= (0.5, 0.5, 0)$?

hints.text: Volatility is the square root: $\sqrt{0.0325} \approx 0.1803$.

feedback.correct: $\sqrt{0.0325} = 18.03\%$, inside the 20% budget. Drag A and B around inside the curve: Q never leaves.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute the variance $\sum \sigma_i^2 w_i^2$, then take its square root.

byKey.var: 0.0325 is the variance. Volatility is its square root, 18.03%.
byKey.avg: You averaged 20% and 30%. Uncorrelated risks partly cancel, so the volatility is lower.

explain.text: $\mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{w} = 0.04(0.25) + 0.09(0.25) = 0.0325$, so the volatility is 18.03%. The budget set is the inside of an ellipse, which is convex. Every mix of two in-budget portfolios stays in budget.

screens.title: At least 28%
screens.prose: A client wants a risky book: volatility **at least** 28%. That looks like the budget with the sign turned. Take $(0, 1, 0)$ at 30% and $(0, 0, 1)$ at 40%; both qualify.

state.caption: The curve is volatility 28%. The set asked for is outside it.

screens.question: What is the volatility of their midpoint $(0, \tfrac12, \tfrac12)$?

hints.text: Variance of the midpoint: $0.09 \times 0.25 + 0.16 \times 0.25$.

feedback.correct: 25%, below 28%. Both ends are in the set and the midpoint is not, so **at least 28%** is not convex.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute the midpoint's variance, then its square root.

byKey.avg: You averaged 30% and 40%. Mixing uncorrelated assets lowers risk, so the midpoint drops to 25% and leaves the set.
byKey.var: 0.0625 is the variance. Its square root is 25%.

explain.text: The midpoint has variance $0.0625$ and volatility 25%, so it falls inside the 28% curve. The riskier set is the outside of an ellipse, and the outside has a hole in it. Flipping $\le$ to $\ge$ on a convex function gives a set that need not be convex, as here.

screens.title: Below 15%
screens.prose: The least risky fully invested portfolio is $(\tfrac{36}{61}, \tfrac{16}{61}, \tfrac{9}{61})$, with volatility 15.364%. A mandate asks for $\mathbf{1}^T\mathbf{w} = 1$ and volatility at most 15%.

state.caption: Curves at volatility 16%, 18% and 20% shrink towards the least risky portfolio.

screens.question: Is that set of portfolios convex?

options.text: Yes. It is empty, and the empty set has no segment that could leave it.
No. It has no points, so it cannot pass the test.
options.why: You read 'no segments' as a failure. The test asks every segment to stay inside; with none, nothing fails.

options.text: We cannot tell without running a solver.
options.why: We can tell: no portfolio beats 15.364%, so the set is empty, and empty sets are convex.

hints.text: Is any fully invested portfolio below 15%?
The least risky one has 15.364%.
So the set is empty. Ask whether an empty set can fail the segment test.

feedback.correct: The set is empty, and the empty set is convex. So is a single point: at a 15.364% limit the set is just the least risky portfolio.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. First decide whether the set has any points.

byKey.fails: The definition says every segment stays inside. With no points there is no segment to fail.
byKey.solver: The least risky portfolio already tells us: 15.364% is above 15%.

explain.text: No fully invested portfolio has volatility below 15.364%, so the set is empty. The empty set and a single point are convex, since no segment can leave them. Convex does not mean feasible.

screens.title: Test it in code
screens.prose: Write three functions. `mix(a, b, theta)` returns $\theta\mathbf{a} + (1 - \theta)\mathbf{b}$ as a list. `in_capped_simplex(w, cap)` checks long-only, a sum of 1 and every weight at most `cap`, within `tol`. `segment_stays_in(member, a, b, n)` tests $n + 1$ evenly spaced points.
screens.question: Complete the three functions. The tests use the discs and the ellipse from the first screens.

widget.how: Submit runs 10 hidden tests in pure Python. Lists are compared entry by entry with math.isclose (relative 1e-9); True and False exactly.

hints.text: `mix` is one list comprehension over `zip(a, b)`.
For the cap test, check the sum first, then every weight against `-tol` and `cap + tol`.
`segment_stays_in` calls `member(mix(a, b, k / n))` for `k` from 0 to `n`.

feedback.correct: All three pass. The two disc centres fail at $k = 1$, the midpoint, as on the first screen.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the failing row: it names the call and what came back.

explain.text: `segment_stays_in` samples the definition: it can find a failure but never proves convexity. The discs fail at the midpoint, so 2 steps find it. A proof still needs the argument of the earlier screen.

screens.title: At most two names
screens.prose: A mandate allows **at most two names** out of three assets. The portfolios $(\tfrac12, \tfrac12, 0)$ and $(0, \tfrac12, \tfrac12)$ both obey it.

state.caption: Two-name portfolios sit on the edges of the triangle.

screens.question: What is their midpoint? Give it as a vector $(w_1, w_2, w_3)$.

hints.text: Average each weight: $\tfrac12(\tfrac12 + 0)$ and so on.
$w_1 = \tfrac14$, $w_2 = \tfrac12$, $w_3 = \tfrac14$.
The midpoint is $(\tfrac14, \tfrac12, \tfrac14)$: three names.

feedback.correct: $(\tfrac14, \tfrac12, \tfrac14)$ holds three names. The mandate's set is the triangle's edges, which is not convex.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take half of each portfolio and add them entry by entry.

byKey.added: You added the two portfolios. The midpoint takes half of each.
byKey.length: Give all three weights, $(w_1, w_2, w_3)$.

explain.text: The midpoint $(\tfrac14, \tfrac12, \tfrac14)$ holds all three names, so a limit on the number of names is not convex. Such limits turn the problem into a search over which names to hold. That is why optimisers with them are slow.

ideas: A set is convex when the segment $\theta\mathbf{a} + (1 - \theta)\mathbf{b}$, $0 \le \theta \le 1$, between any two of its points stays in it.
Half-spaces, the long-only simplex and risk budgets $\mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{w} \le c$ are convex, and so is any intersection of convex sets.
A floor on volatility, an exact volatility and a limit on the number of names are not convex. The empty set and a single point are.

formula.name: Convex set
formula.note: Every pair and every $\theta$, not only the midpoint.

summary.trap: Volatility at least 28% looks like a budget, but the midpoint of 30% and 40% portfolios has 25%.

quiz.prose: Let $R = \{(x, y) : 1 \le x^2 + y^2 \le 4\}$, a ring.
quiz.question: Is $R$ convex?

options.text: No: $(1.5, 0)$ and $(-1.5, 0)$ are in $R$, and their midpoint, the origin, is not.
Yes: it is bounded by two circles, and discs are convex.
options.why: You judged by the boundary curves. The hole between them is what breaks the segment test.

options.text: Yes: it is symmetric about the origin.
options.why: Symmetry is not convexity. The segment through the hole leaves the ring.

feedback.correct: The segment from $(1.5, 0)$ to $(-1.5, 0)$ passes through the hole.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for two points on opposite sides of the hole.

explain.text: Both points have $x^2 + y^2 = 2.25$, inside the ring. Their midpoint has $x^2 + y^2 = 0$, inside the hole, so $R$ is not convex.

quiz.question: What is the first weight of $\theta\mathbf{a} + (1 - \theta)\mathbf{b}$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight $\mathbf{a}$ by 0.25 and $\mathbf{b}$ by 0.75.

byKey.added: You added $0.2 + 0.6$. A mix weights them.

quiz.prose: Each set below is a set of fully invested portfolios of the three running assets.
quiz.question: Which set is convex?

options.why: You flipped the sign of a convex constraint. The outside of an ellipse has a hole, as the 28% screen showed.
A curve is not convex: the midpoint of two points on it falls inside.
The midpoint of two two-name portfolios can hold three names.

feedback.correct: At most 25% is the inside of an ellipse.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which set is a filled region with no dent?

explain.text: $\mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{w} \le 0.0625$ is the filled ellipse, convex. The others fail. The outside has a hole, the curve misses its midpoints, and the edge set has a gap.

quiz.question: Which line shows that $\theta\mathbf{x} + (1 - \theta)\mathbf{y} \in H$ for $0 \le \theta \le 1$?

options.why: That checks the midpoint only. The claim is for every $\theta$.
That is about the sum, not the mix. Divide by 2 and it is the midpoint case only.

feedback.correct: Linearity splits the product, and each piece is at most its share of $b$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use linearity of $\mathbf{a}^T$ and keep $\theta$ general.

explain.text: $\mathbf{a}^T$ is linear, so the mix gives $\theta\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{x} + (1 - \theta)\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{y}$. Each term is at most $\theta b$ or $(1 - \theta)b$ because $\theta$ and $1 - \theta$ are nonnegative.
